newsitem.title: GERMANY: British pop groups battle for book fair rights.
newsitem.headline: British pop groups battle for book fair rights.

text.p: The Rolling Stones battled with young pretenders Oasis on Tuesday for top pop honours at the world's biggest book fair.
This time the two are bursting into print, not song, as the rights to new biographies are offered at the Frankfurt fair which has attracted 9,000 publishers from 105 countries.
The Rolling Stones, the self-styled "greatest rock 'n' roll band in the world", are telling the story of their three decades on the road.
Oasis hit the headlines last month when their U.S tour collapsed amid reports that singer Liam Gallagher and his guitarist brother Noel had come to blows. Now their brother Paul tells all.
Virgin Publishing, the book arm of British entrepreneur Richard Branson's empire, is in the enviable position of drumming up international business for both books.
"This is as close as you can get to huge rock bands," the publishers' managing director Rob Shreeve told Reuters.
The differences across the generation gap are stark.
The Rolling Stones, whose illustrated official history is being compiled by singer Jools Holland, revel in touring live.
Singer Mick Jagger, still swivelling hips and pouting lips at 53, has said of their 30 years of live shows: "I like it on the road. If I couldn't go out there, I think I would go mad."
He spent last week at his south of France home taping for Holland his memories of the group. The book will be published in autumn 1997 but Virgin are already negotiating rights.
Oasis, whose first two albums sold 20 million copies, have led a "Britpop" revival to echo the Sixties heyday of The Beatles and the Stones.
But now they are quitting live performances to concentrate on producing a third album.
They delight in being the wild boys of modern pop with Liam and Noel constantly bad-mouthing each other and the press.
Their brother Paul's biography gives a blow-by-blow account of the years of feuding and is already a bestseller in Britain.
But what were the chances of repeating its home-grown success at Frankfurt where 80 percent of global book right deals are struck each year?

"Ironically American publishers are already very interested despite the tantrums the group threw there. Oasis are very big in lots of European markets too. This is a special book as it is that close to them," Shreeve said.
